newsitem.title: USA: Paying bills online is latest home banking wrinkle.
newsitem.headline: Paying bills online is latest home banking wrinkle.

text.p: It's no secret that getting people to pay bills online has been tough.

Although they've been around for years, online bill payment offered through banks and software programmes such as Quicken and Microsoft Money haven't caught on as quickly as other home-banking applications, for any number of reasons.

In many cases, remittances take as long to be delivered as paper checks, or longer. Although they start out electronic, a majority of online payments -- up to 80 percent according to some analysts -- still are printed out and mailed to merchants. Services can be awkward to learn and some charge a monthly fee, a big turn off for consumers.
But the powers behind electronic banking believe they've hit on just the thing to make online bill payment take off, and it goes by the very unglamourous name of online bill presentment.
In layman's terms, online bill presentment means someone can go to a Web site, see a detailed, graphical representation of a bill, pay it, and have the payment electronically forwarded to the biller.

Unlike paper bills, online bills are interactive, so someone scanning their phone bill, for example, could itemise calls by area code or see how many times a month their teenager called a friend in a different town.
"It's the Holy Grail of online bill payment," said Karen Epper, online banking analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass.
A number of companies with stakes in online banking's success are testing online bill presentment with major utilities, phone companies and other merchants.

CheckFree (http://www.checkfree.com) and CyberCash (http://www.cybercash.com) are running pilot programmes and expect to offer the services on a limited basis to the general public later this year. Visa (www.visa.com) plans to begin consumer tests of its E-Pay programme in late 1997 or early next year.

Other companies that have publicly discussed plans to provide bill presentment solutions include InteliData (http://www.intelidata.com), Home Financial Network (http://www.homeatm.com), International Billing Services (http://www.billing.com), and BlueGill Technologies (http://www.bluegill.com).
Forrester's Epper gives the early lead to CheckFree, a leading electronic payments processor that handles online bill payment for 1.3 million consumers and 224 financial institutions.
Atlanta-based CheckFree launched its E-Bill programme last month with 10 merchant customers, including BellSouth, Columbia Gas, Florida Power & Light and the Small Business Administration.

In ongoing pilot tests with those billers, consumers log onto a special CheckFree Web site (http://getbills.com) to see their bills, but links from E-Bill to online bill payment won't be added until June.

Once enough merchants have signed on, CheckFree will approach banks to assume hosting duties, reasoning that consumers would rather deal with their financial institution than a behind-the-scenes processor.

CheckFree makes its money by collecting transaction fees from utilities and merchants who use E-Bill to transmit bills to customers, and also by collecting transactions fees from banks whose customers use the service to pay bills.

CyberCash, a Reston, Va., Internet payment specialist, rolled out its PayNow electronic bill-pay service in late January, and expects four partners to complete beta tests by early spring before marketing it in the second half of 1997.

Unlike E-Bill, CyberCash believes consumers will want to pay bills at the Web site of their phone company, electric company or mortgage underwriter, not their bank, and is structuring pilots accordingly.

One CyberCash partner, bill processor Princeton Telecom Corp., in Princeton, N.J., expects to complete a two-month pilot test this month before offering PayNow to companies that currently use its telephone bill-pay programme.

International Billing Services, in El Dorado, Calif., one of the largest billing outsourcers in the country, tested PayNow with a major, unidentified telephone company during the first quarter, and is recruiting customers. Another partner, Electronic Funds & Data, in Bridgehampton, N.Y., is offering PayNow through its BillSite Web-based bill-pay service.

Visa is working with existing bank customers to sign up billers for its E-Pay service, but won't begin consumer tests until later this year. Like CheckFree, the company will put banks in the driver's seat, by offering E-Pay through bank Web sites or through links to personal financial management software.
On the software side, online bill payment could get a boost next fall, with the release of new versions of Quicken and Money 97 that will include new industry standards for bill presentment.

"So in Quicken, for example, you'll have a button or icon that flashes and says you have a bill, you'd click on it, it picks up the bills at the (Web) site and brings them to you to pay," said Matt Lewis, a CheckFree spokesman.
Ultimately, that kind of so-called "push" technology will be critical to widespread acceptance of online bill presentment and payment, industry insiders said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
